mainTopic: Nullifying a גוי's idol, the brick law learned from the אשרות and the עגל, abandoned idols, and kings' platforms
overview: The amud opens with the end of a ברייתא: a גוי's idol is not nullified when the owners leave it but plan to return, like the nations in יהושע's war. The גמרא explains why all four cases in that ברייתא had to be listed: borrowing against the idol, a rockslide covering it, robbers stealing it, and owners leaving it behind and going overseas. It then asks why the war of יהושע is mentioned at all. It answers that this hints to רב's law: a גוי who bows to a brick a Jew set up for worship makes it forbidden. The source is the burning of the אשרות in ארץ ישראל, and the reason given is that after the עגל the gentiles' worship counted as done on the Jews' behalf. A new משנה follows: an idol abandoned in peacetime is permitted, one abandoned in wartime is forbidden, and kings' platforms are permitted. רב applies the peacetime rule to בית נמרוד, and רבי יוחנן explains the reason given for the platforms. The amud ends with עולא sitting on a damaged platform. רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש permit a damaged platform, but a damaged altar stays forbidden until most of it is destroyed.

steps.title: If the owners plan to come back, the idol keeps its status
steps.stepSummary: The closing line of the ברייתא: when owners leave their idol behind but expect to return, as in the war of יהושע, the idol is not nullified.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the owners are going to come back, like what happened in the war of יהושע, the idol is not nullified.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the last line of a ברייתא that started earlier. It says that if the owners left but plan to come back, the idol still counts as עבודה זרה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Leaving an idol behind is not enough to cancel its status. What matters is whether the owner has really given it up. If he expects to return, he still sees it as his object of worship, so there is no ביטול.

keyTerms.meaning: Nullified; an idol that has lost its status as עבודה זרה
The war of Joshua, when בני ישראל conquered ארץ ישראל
Idol worship, or an object used for idol worship

steps.confusionAlert: This is not the start of a new teaching. It is the end of a ברייתא whose earlier cases appear just before this point. The גמרא's discussion that follows is about all of those cases together.

phrases.english: If they are going to return
phrases.notes: "They" means the owners of the idol, who left it behind.

phrases.english: as in the war of Joshua
phrases.notes: Like the nations who fled from יהושע's army. They left, but they meant to come back.

phrases.english: it is not nullified.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the ברייתא begun before this section
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An idol left behind by owners who intend to return is not nullified.

steps.title: Why the rockslide case is needed after the borrowing case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins its צריכותא. The borrowing case alone would not teach the rockslide case, because not clearing the rocks could look like giving the idol up.
steps.simpleTranslation: And all the cases are needed. If it had only taught that he borrowed against it, we would say: since he did not sell it, he did not nullify it. But when a rockslide fell on it, since he is not clearing it away, you might say he nullified it. So that case is needed too.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the ברייתא needed to list more than one case. It starts with the first two: borrowing against the idol, and a rockslide falling on it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Borrowing against the idol clearly shows he wants to keep it, since he did not sell it. In the rockslide case the owner does nothing, and leaving it buried might look like he gave up on it. So the ברייתא had to teach that even here it is not nullified.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed. The opening word of a צריכותא, which explains why several similar cases all had to be taught
He borrowed money against it, using the idol as security
A rockslide or collapse of rubble
You might say. It introduces a mistaken assumption

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read "say he nullified it" as the law. It is the mistake we might have made, and the ברייתא rules against it.

phrases.english: And it is necessary
phrases.notes: Necessary to teach all the cases. The גמרא is answering an unspoken question: why not just teach one?

phrases.english: for if it had taught only "he borrowed against it"
since he did not sell it, he did not nullify it;
but when "a rockslide fell on it"
since he is not clearing it away,
you might say he nullified it; so it is necessary.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the ברייתא listed several cases instead of one
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The rockslide case is needed because doing nothing about the rubble might look like giving up the idol.

steps.title: Why the robbery case is needed after the rockslide case
steps.stepSummary: The rockslide case alone would not teach the robbery case. A buried idol is still safe and easy to reach, while not chasing after stolen goods might look like giving up.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if it had only taught that a rockslide fell on it, we would say that is because he thinks: here it lies, and whenever I want it, I'll take it. But when robbers stole it, since he is not searching for it, he nullified it. So that case is needed too.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues the chain. It shows why the robbery case could not be learned from the rockslide case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the rockslide case the owner has a good reason to wait, because the idol is safe under the rocks. When robbers take it and he does not go looking for it, that looks more like giving up. So the ברייתא had to teach that this, too, is not ביטול.

phrases.english: And if it had taught only "a rockslide fell on it"
we would say that is because he thinks: here it lies,

phrases.aramaic: כֹּל אֵימַת דְּבָעֵינָא לַהּ שָׁקֵילְנָא לַהּ,
phrases.english: whenever I want it, I will take it;
but when "robbers stole it"
since he is not searching after it
you might say he nullified it; so it is necessary.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next link in the צריכותא chain
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The robbery case is needed because not chasing after a stolen idol might look like giving it up.

steps.title: Why the overseas case is needed after the robbery case
steps.stepSummary: The robbery case alone would not teach the overseas case. A stolen idol will still be worshipped by someone, but owners who choose to leave it behind seem to have truly given it up.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if it had only taught that robbers stole it, we would say that is because he thinks: if a gentile took it, he will surely worship it; if a Jew took it, since it is very valuable, he will sell it to a gentile, who will worship it. But when the owners left it and went overseas, since they did not take it with them, you might say they nullified it. So that case is needed too.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the last link of the chain. The גמרא shows why the overseas case could not be learned from the robbery case, which completes the explanation of all four cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: After a robbery the owner can comfort himself that the idol will still be worshipped wherever it ends up, so his silence is not giving it up. Leaving it behind on purpose is the strongest sign of all that he does not care about it. That is why the ברייתא had to say that even this is not ביטול, as long as the owners plan to return.
steps.whatToRemember: The four cases form a ladder: borrowing, rockslide, robbery, going overseas. Each one looks more like giving up the idol than the one before, yet none of them counts as ביטול. The owner's own act of giving it up is what nullifies an idol.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that ביטול depends on the owner's real intention, not on outward neglect. Even leaving the idol behind is not enough if the owner plans to come back.

phrases.english: And if it had taught only "robbers stole it"
we would say that is because he thinks:
if a gentile took it
he will surely worship it,
if a Jew took it
since its value is high
he will sell it to a gentile, who will worship it;
but when "the owners left it
and went overseas"
since they did not take it with them
you might say they nullified it; so it is necessary.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Final link in the צריכותא chain, which ties back to the overseas case in step 1
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: All four cases are needed. Each one rules out a mistaken idea that the case before it could not rule out, and the overseas case is the strongest.

steps.title: Did anyone return after the war of יהושע?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא re-quotes the ברייתא's line about the war of יהושע. It challenges the wording, since the Canaanites never returned home.
steps.simpleTranslation: The ברייתא said: If they will return in the future, as in the war of יהושע, the idol is not nullified. The גמרא asks: Did the people in the war of יהושע actually return?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the ברייתא's words and points out a problem with them: in the war of יהושע, the enemy never came back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא's wording sounds like the war of יהושע is an example of owners who came back. But the Canaanites were defeated, so the comparison seems wrong. The גמרא needs to explain what the ברייתא really means.

keyTerms.meaning: The war of יהושע, when בני ישראל conquered ארץ ישראל

phrases.english: If they will return in the future, as in the war of יהושע,
it is not nullified.
Is it so that in the war of יהושע they returned?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the צריכותא, the גמרא returns to the ברייתא's closing line from step 1 and challenges its wording.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The phrase suggests the owners in the war of יהושע returned, but historically they did not.

steps.title: The ברייתא is making a comparison
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא means that owners who plan to return have the same status as the idols in the war of יהושע, and their idol is not nullified.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what it means: If they plan to return, it is like the war of יהושע, and it has no nullification.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by reading the ברייתא differently. The war of יהושע is not an example of people returning. It is a comparison for the law.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Canaanites in the war of יהושע planned to come back, even though they never did. So their idols were never given up. Any owners who plan to return are treated the same way.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it is saying (a re-reading of the text)

phrases.english: This is what it is saying:
If they will return in the future,
it is like the war of יהושע,
and it has no nullification.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 5 by re-reading the ברייתא.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to say that the owners in the war of יהושע actually returned.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא compares the law of owners who plan to return to the idols in the war of יהושע, which were not nullified.

steps.title: Why mention the war of יהושע at all?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא needed to connect this law to the war of יהושע.
steps.simpleTranslation: And why do I need to connect it to the war of יהושע?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a follow-up question. The ברייתא could have simply said that owners who plan to return do not nullify their idol, so why bring in the war of יהושע?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The law makes sense without any example. So mentioning the war of יהושע must be teaching something extra. The גמרא is setting up the next step, where it explains what that extra lesson is.

keyTerms.meaning: To connect it to, to hang it on

phrases.english: And why do I need to connect it to the war of יהושע?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Now that the comparison is understood, the גמרא asks why the comparison is needed.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What extra lesson comes from mentioning the war of יהושע

steps.title: A side lesson: a גוי can forbid a Jew's brick
steps.stepSummary: The mention teaches in passing that laws of עבודה זרה can be learned from the war of יהושע. This connects to רב's rule that a גוי who bows to a brick a Jew set up makes it forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: It teaches us something in passing, like what רב יהודה said in the name of רב: A Jew who stood up a brick in order to bow to it, and then a גוי came and bowed to it, the גוי made it forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the war of יהושע is mentioned to teach a side lesson. It then quotes רב's law about the brick, which is learned from the war of יהושע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a person cannot make forbidden something that does not belong to him. Yet רב says the גוי makes the Jew's brick forbidden. The source for this comes from the war of יהושע, which is why the ברייתא mentions it.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a real halacha: a Jew who prepares an object for worship gives a גוי who bows to it the power to forbid it, even though the object is not the גוי's.

phrases.aramaic: מִלְּתָא אַגַּב אוֹרְחֵאּ קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן,
phrases.english: It teaches us a matter in passing,

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הָא דְּאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: like that which רב יהודה said in the name of רב:
A Jew who stood up a brick
in order to bow to it,
and a gentile came and bowed to it,
he made it forbidden.
phrases.notes: This is surprising, because the brick belongs to the Jew, not the גוי.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִלְּתָא אַגַּב אוֹרְחֵיהּ קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 7 and opens a new topic: רב's law of the brick.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The war of יהושע is mentioned to hint that laws of עבודה זרה, like רב's law of the brick, are learned from it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A גוי who bows to a brick a Jew set up for worship makes it forbidden.

steps.title: What is the source for the brick law?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how we know that the גוי makes the Jew's brick forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where do we know that he makes it forbidden?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for a source for רב's law. This sets up רבי אלעזר's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The law goes against the usual rule that a person can only forbid what he owns. So the גמרא wants to see where it comes from.

phrases.english: From where do we know that he makes it forbidden?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the law quoted in step 8.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source showing that a גוי can forbid an object that is not his

steps.title: רבי אלעזר: learn it from the אשרות in ארץ ישראל
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר says the source is from the beginning of ארץ ישראל. The תורה commanded burning the Canaanites' אשרות, even though the land belonged to the Jews.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said: It is like the beginning of ארץ ישראל, since the תורה says 'and you shall burn their אשרות with fire.' But the land was the Jews' inheritance from their fathers, and a person cannot forbid something that is not his!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר brings a source from the conquest of ארץ ישראל in the days of יהושע. The trees the Canaanites worshipped had to be burned, so they were forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The land, and the trees on it, belonged to the Jews as an inheritance from their fathers. Yet the תורה orders the Canaanites' אשרות burned, as if their worship had made those trees forbidden. That clashes with the rule that a person cannot forbid what is not his. רבי אלעזר ends with this difficulty, and steps 11–13 explain how the trees still became forbidden, which is also the source for the brick.

keyTerms.meaning: Like the beginning, when בני ישראל entered the land
Trees that were worshipped as idols

keyTerms.term: אֵין אָדָם אוֹסֵר דָּבָר שֶׁאֵינוֹ שֶׁלּוֹ
keyTerms.meaning: A person cannot forbid something that is not his

phrases.english: רבי אלעזר said:
It is like the beginning of ארץ ישראל,
phrases.notes: He means the time when בני ישראל first came into the land with יהושע.

phrases.english: for the Merciful One said:
"And their אשרות you shall burn with fire,"
Now, it is an inheritance to them from their fathers,

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵין אָדָם אוֹסֵר דָּבָר שֶׁאֵינוֹ שֶׁלּוֹ!
phrases.english: and a person cannot forbid something that is not his!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר: כַּתְּחִילָּה שֶׁל אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 9 by bringing a source from the war of יהושע.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The source is the command to burn the Canaanites' אשרות on land that belonged to the Jews. The גמרא then works out how those trees became forbidden: through agency created by the עגל (steps 11–13).
steps.raayaObject: רב's law that a גוי forbids a Jew's brick

steps.title: The trees worshipped before the land was given don't explain the verse
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the idea that the verse only means trees worshipped before the land became the Jews'. Those would only need a simple nullification, not burning.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say the verse is talking about the trees that were worshipped from the very beginning, a simple nullification would be enough for them!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא blocks a way someone might try to explain away רבי אלעזר's proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone might say the burned trees were ones the Canaanites worshipped originally, before the land was given to the Jews, so they could forbid them. But an idol of a גוי can be fixed by nullification, so it would not need to be burned. Since the תורה demands burning, this explanation fails, and the גמרא needs a different reason, which comes in step 12.
steps.confusionAlert: This line is not attacking רבי אלעזר. It is rejecting an alternative explanation of the verse, which makes his proof stronger.
steps.whatToRemember: The burning of the אשרות cannot be explained as trees worshipped before the land was given to the Jews, because a גוי's idol needs only ביטול. The next step gives the real reason.

phrases.english: And if it is because of those from the very beginning,
phrases.notes: These are trees worshipped before the land was given to the Jews, when it still belonged to the Canaanites.

phrases.english: a simple nullification would be enough for them!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends רבי אלעזר's proof by ruling out another reading of the verse.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The suggestion that the burned אשרות were only trees worshipped before the land became the Jews'
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Such trees belonged to the גוי when worshipped, so nullification would be enough, yet the תורה requires burning.

steps.title: The Golden Calf made later gentile worship count as the Jews' worship
steps.stepSummary: Because the Jews worshipped the עגל, they showed they were open to עבודה זרה. Gentiles who later worshipped were acting as their agents.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, since the Jews worshipped the Calf, they showed they were comfortable with idol worship. So when the gentiles came and worshipped, they were acting as the Jews' agents.
steps.whatsHappening: Step 11 rejected the first explanation. Now the גמרא gives a new reason why the תורה required burning the אשרות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worship of the עגל revealed that the Jewish people wanted עבודה זרה. So when גוים worshipped trees in ארץ ישראל, it counted as if they were doing it on the Jews' behalf. That makes these trees like a Jew's idol, and a Jew's idol can never be canceled; it must be burned.

keyTerms.meaning: They were comfortable with it, they wanted it
Agency, acting on someone else's behalf

steps.confusionAlert: The גוים were not actually appointed by anyone. The גמרא means that since the Jews showed they wanted idol worship, the gentiles' worship counts as if it were done for them.

phrases.english: Rather, since the Jewish people worshipped the Calf,
they revealed their intentions
that they were comfortable with idol worship.
And when the gentiles came [and worshipped],
they were carrying out their agency.
phrases.notes: "Their" means the Jews'. The gentiles were acting for them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the explanation rejected in step 11 with a new explanation of the אשרות verse.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New mechanism: agency created by the Jews' revealed desire for עבודה זרה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The burning was because the trees were worshipped before the land belonged to the Jews, which was rejected.
steps.terutzMaskana: The גוים' worship counted as the Jews' worship because of the עגל, so the trees had the status of a Jew's idol.

steps.title: Applying the same logic to the Jew's brick
steps.stepSummary: A Jew who set up a brick showed he wanted עבודה זרה. A גוי who worships it is acting as his agent.
steps.simpleTranslation: So too, a Jew who set up a brick showed he is comfortable with idol worship. When a gentile comes and worships it, he is acting as the Jew's agent.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא takes the עגל principle and applies it to רב's case of the brick from step 8, which answers the question from step 9.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Setting up the brick shows the Jew wants idol worship, just as the עגל showed for the whole nation. So the גוי's bowing counts as done for the Jew, and the brick becomes forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: Set up a brick upright, intending to bow to it
So too, the same applies here

steps.whatToRemember: A גוי's worship can forbid a Jew's object when the Jew has already shown he wants it for idol worship. The source is the עגל and the אשרות of ארץ ישראל.

phrases.english: So too, a Jew who set up a brick
revealed his intention
that he is comfortable with idol worship.
And when a gentile came and worshipped it,
he is carrying out his agency.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the principle from step 12 to רב's brick case.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How do we know a גוי can forbid a Jew's brick (step 9)?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Just as the Jews' desire at the עגל made gentile worship count for them, the Jew's setting up of the brick makes the גוי his agent.

steps.title: Maybe they only wanted the Calf
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges that the Jews may have only wanted the עגל and no other idols.
steps.simpleTranslation: But perhaps they only wanted the Calf, and not anything else?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the proof by suggesting the Jews' desire was limited to the עגל itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the Jews only wanted the עגל, then gentiles worshipping trees were not doing what the Jews wanted. If so, the agency idea would not work for the אשרות.

phrases.english: But perhaps it was the Calf that they were comfortable with,
but with anything else, not?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reach of the principle from step 12.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the Jews were open to עבודה זרה in general
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The עגל shows a desire only for the עגל, so it cannot make gentile tree-worship count as the Jews' worship.

steps.title: The verse says 'gods' in plural
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק says "These are your gods," in the plural, which shows they wanted many gods.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse says: "These are your gods, Israel." This teaches that they desired many gods.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from a פסוק about the עגל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word "gods" is plural, even though the עגל was one object. This shows the Jews wanted idol worship in general, not just the עגל. So the agency idea still works.

phrases.english: The verse says:
"These are your gods, Israel"
This teaches that they desired many gods.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 14.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The Jews only wanted the עגל.
steps.terutzMaskana: The plural "gods" shows they wanted many idols, so any gentile worship counts.

steps.title: Maybe only trees worshipped at the time of the Calf are forbidden
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that only trees worshipped while the Jews were worshipping the עגל should be forbidden. Later ones should be permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: Say that whatever was worshipped together with the Calf is forbidden, but from then on, they should be permitted?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a new challenge about timing: the agency should only last while the Jews actually wanted idols.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the Jews did תשובה, they no longer wanted idol worship. So any אשרה worshipped afterward should not count as the Jews' worship and should be permitted with simple nullification.

keyTerms.meaning: Together with, at the same time as

phrases.english: Say: whatever [was worshipped] together with the Calf should be forbidden,
but from here on, they should be permitted?
phrases.notes: "From here on" means after the עגל, once the Jews stopped wanting idols.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 15 settled what the Jews wanted, this challenges how long that agency lasted.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that all the אשרות needed burning
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The agency should only cover worship done during the עגל period, not later worship.

steps.title: No one can tell which trees were worshipped when
steps.stepSummary: There is no way to prove which אשרות were worshipped at the time of the עגל, so all must be burned.
steps.simpleTranslation: Who can prove [which ones were worshipped when]?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers briefly: since we cannot tell the trees apart, all of them are forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא accepts that in theory only trees from the עגל period are a Jew's idol. But since no one can identify which trees those are, the תורה required burning all of them.
steps.whatToRemember: All the אשרות in ארץ ישראל had to be burned, because some were worshipped as the Jews' agents during the עגל and no one can tell which ones.

phrases.english: Who can prove [which ones]?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Practical uncertainty: we cannot tell the trees apart
steps.terutzMaskana: Since no one can tell which trees date to the עגל period, all are forbidden.

steps.title: An idol left behind in peace or in war
steps.stepSummary: An idol abandoned by its worshippers in peacetime is permitted. One abandoned in wartime is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: An idol that its worshippers left behind: in peacetime it is permitted, in wartime it is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It rules on an idol that its worshippers left behind.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Leaving an idol behind in peacetime is a free choice, so it counts as giving it up. In wartime, people flee and are forced to leave things behind, so it does not show they gave the idol up.

keyTerms.meaning: They left it behind, abandoned it

phrases.english: Mishnah:
An idol that its worshippers left behind:
in peacetime, it is permitted;
in wartime, it is forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new משנה, beginning a new topic after the previous discussion ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An abandoned idol is permitted if left in peacetime and forbidden if left in wartime.

steps.title: Kings' platforms are permitted
steps.stepSummary: Stone platforms used to hold idols when kings pass by are permitted, since the idol is only placed there at those times.
steps.simpleTranslation: Platforms of kings are permitted, because they set the idol on them only at the time that the kings pass by.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues with a second ruling, about the platforms where idols are set up in honor of passing kings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The platform itself is not worshipped. It is only a stand that sometimes holds an idol when a king passes by, so the platform stays permitted.

phrases.english: Platforms of kings:
these are permitted,
because they set it up
phrases.notes: "It" means the idol, which is placed on the platform.

phrases.english: at the time that the kings pass by.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second ruling in the same משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Kings' platforms are permitted, since the idol is only placed on them when kings pass by.

steps.title: בית נמרוד Is Like an Idol Abandoned in Peacetime
steps.stepSummary: רב rules that בית נמרוד counts as an idol abandoned by its worshippers in peacetime, so it is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה בר אבא says in the name of רב: The temple of נמרוד counts as an idol its worshippers left in peacetime, so it is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings רב's ruling that applies the משנה's peacetime/wartime rule (step 18) to a famous site, בית נמרוד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 18 taught that an idol abandoned in peacetime is permitted, because the worshippers gave it up by choice. רב puts בית נמרוד in that permitted group. This sets up the obvious question of why it is not 'wartime', since the builders were driven away.

keyTerms.meaning: The temple of נמרוד, meaning what is left of מגדל בבל
Peacetime, when people leave by choice

phrases.aramaic: גְּמָ׳ אָמַר רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: GEMARA: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba says that Rav says:
The temple of Nimrod is
phrases.notes: This is מגדל בבל. See בראשית 11:1–9.

phrases.english: like an idol that its worshippers abandoned
in peacetime, and it is permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the peacetime/wartime abandonment rule of step 18 to בית נמרוד.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בית נמרוד is treated as abandoned in peacetime and is permitted.

steps.title: Why the Scattering at Babel Still Counts as Peacetime
steps.stepSummary: Even though ה׳ forcibly scattered the builders, they could have come back. Since they did not, they gave up their idol by choice.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even though ה׳ scattering them looks like wartime, if they had wanted to come back they could have. Since they never came back, they nullified it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers a question it does not spell out: being forced out by ה׳ sounds like wartime, so why is it permitted?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wartime abandonment does not cancel an idol, because the worshippers never chose to leave it. Here, even if the leaving was forced, the builders were free to return later. Not returning shows they chose to give it up, and that is a real ביטול.

keyTerms.meaning: Wartime, when people leave by force

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the deciding factor is whether the worshippers chose to give up the idol, not just how they first left.

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל גַּב דְּכִי בַּדְּרִינְהוּ רַחֲמָנָא
phrases.english: Even though when the Merciful One scattered them
it resembles wartime,
if they had wanted to return, they could have returned;
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets; the word in square brackets is the corrected wording. Both mean 'wanted'.

phrases.english: since they did not return, they nullified it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַף עַל גַּב דְּכִי בַּדְּרִינְהוּ רַחֲמָנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends רב's ruling against a question the גמרא leaves unstated: forced scattering looks like wartime.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the case: the abandonment became voluntary once they could return and chose not to.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Being scattered by ה׳ is forced, like wartime, so the idol should stay forbidden.
steps.terutzMaskana: Because they could have returned and did not, they gave it up by choice, so it is permitted.

steps.title: Questioning the משנה's Reason for Permitting Kings' Platforms
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about kings' platforms and asks how the fact that idols are placed on them when kings pass by could make them permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: kings' stone platforms are permitted. But is that a reason? Just because they place the idol there when the kings pass by, they should be permitted?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the משנה's ruling again in order to question its reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 19 gave the משנה's reason: the idol is placed on the platform only when kings pass by. The גמרא asks why that should help. The platform is still used to hold an idol, so that reason alone seems to point toward forbidding it.

keyTerms.meaning: Stone platforms on which idols were placed
Is it really because...?, a challenge to a reason
That they place or set up

phrases.english: Stone platforms of kings
these are permitted.
But is it because they place it
phrases.notes: 'It' means the idol that is set up on the platform.

phrases.english: at the time the kings pass by that they are permitted?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the משנה's ruling on platforms (step 19) and challenges its reasoning.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's reason for permitting kings' platforms.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Placing an idol on the platform, even sometimes, ties the platform to idol worship. That does not explain why it would be permitted.

steps.title: The Kings Sometimes Skip the Platform Entirely
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן explains that the משנה means the kings sometimes leave this road and take a different one, so the platforms have little importance and are permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר בר חנה said in the name of רבי יוחנן: This is what the משנה means. They set them up for when kings pass by, and the kings sometimes leave this road and take a different one.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן fills in the missing part of the משנה's reason to answer the question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point is not just that the idol is placed there sometimes. The kings may not use that road at all and go a different way. Since the platforms are not treated as important, they are not counted as items serving the idol, so they are permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it means, an explanation of the text

steps.whatToRemember: Kings' platforms are permitted because the kings often go a different way, so the platforms never become important to the idol.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן,
phrases.english: Rabba bar bar Ḥana said that Rabbi Yoḥanan said,
this is what it is saying:
because they place them
at the time that the kings pass by,
and kings leave this road
and go by a different road.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן, הָכִי קָאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 22 by completing the משנה's reason.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterprets the משנה by adding a missing part of its reason.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The only reason is that idols are placed there when kings pass, which seems too weak.
steps.terutzMaskana: Kings often skip that road, so the platform has little importance and is permitted.

steps.title: עולא Sits on a Damaged Platform
steps.stepSummary: When עולא came to בבל, he sat on a damaged idol platform.
steps.simpleTranslation: When עולא came, he sat on a damaged platform.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a short story about עולא's behavior. It sets up רב יהודה's challenge in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sitting on the platform means עולא treated it as allowed for use. Since it was damaged, the story raises a new question: does damage to a platform change its status?

keyTerms.meaning: When עולא came from ארץ ישראל to בבל

phrases.english: When Ulla came,
phrases.notes: He came from ארץ ישראל to בבל.

phrases.english: he sat on a damaged platform.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אֲתָא עוּלָּא, יָתֵיב אַבִּימְסָא פְּגִימָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new case about platforms: one that is damaged.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: עולא's conduct suggests that a damaged platform may be used.

steps.title: רב יהודה Objects: A Damaged Platform Is Forbidden
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה challenges עולא with the ruling of רב and שמואל that a damaged platform stays forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said to עולא: But רב and שמואל both say that a damaged platform is forbidden!
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה challenges what עולא did by quoting a ruling from רב and שמואל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב and שמואל hold that damage does not cancel a platform's forbidden status. If so, עולא should not have sat on it.

keyTerms.meaning: But surely..., opens a challenge from a known source

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said to Ulla:
But don't Rav and Shmuel both say:
A platform that was damaged is forbidden!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב יְהוּדָה לְעוּלָּא: וְהָא רַב וּשְׁמוּאֵל דְּאָמְרִי תַּרְוַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges עולא's conduct from step 24.
steps.kashyaTarget: עולא's sitting on a damaged platform.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב and שמואל rule that a damaged platform remains forbidden, so using it seems wrong.

steps.title: The 'No Worship of Fragments' Idea Does Not Help for Platforms
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה blocks a possible defense: the rule that people do not worship broken pieces applies only to the idol itself, not to a platform.
steps.simpleTranslation: And even according to the one who says people don't worship broken pieces, that is only about an idol, because worshipping broken pieces is degrading. But a platform? He doesn't care if it is damaged!
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה continues his challenge and shuts down a defense עולא might have used.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Some hold that a broken idol loses its status, because no one wants to bow to broken pieces. A damaged platform still does its job of holding the idol, and the worshipper does not mind the damage. So that idea does not save the platform, and the challenge to עולא stands.

keyTerms.meaning: According to the one who says
People do not worship broken pieces

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the idol and the platform. Breaking the idol itself may cancel it for some opinions, but a damaged platform still works, so the same reasoning does not apply.

phrases.english: And even according to the one who says:
people do not worship broken pieces —
that applies only to an idol,
since it is degrading to him to worship broken pieces,
but this, he doesn't care about!
phrases.notes: 'This' is the damaged platform. It still holds the idol just fine.

steps.triggerLanguage: וַאֲפִילּוּ לְמַאן דְּאָמַר: אֵין עוֹבְדִים לִשְׁבָרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Strengthens רב יהודה's challenge by blocking a possible defense of עולא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The possible defense that damage cancels the forbidden status.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The 'broken pieces' idea rests on the degradation of worshipping a broken idol. A damaged platform still works, so its user does not care, and the idea does not apply.

steps.title: עולא relies on רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש
steps.stepSummary: עולא honors רב and שמואל, but he answers that רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש both rule that a damaged platform is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Who would give us the dust of רב and שמואל, so we could fill our eyes with it? But look, רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש both say: a platform that was damaged is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: עולא answers רב יהודה's challenge. He says he is following a different set of great authorities, רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש, who permit a damaged platform.
steps.deeperAnalysis: עולא does not reject רב and שמואל disrespectfully. He speaks of them with huge honor. Still, he shows that his action has a solid source: two great teachers from ארץ ישראל rule against them, so he was allowed to sit on the platform.

keyTerms.meaning: A platform or stone base on which an idol is placed
Dust (here, the dust of their graves)

phrases.english: He said to him:
Who will give us from the dust
of Rav and Shmuel, so we could fill our eyes?
phrases.notes: A way of showing deep honor: even their grave dust would be precious to us.

phrases.english: But look, Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
both say:
A platform that was damaged is permitted,

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מַאן יָהֵיב לַן מֵעַפְרָא דְּרַב וּשְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב יהודה's challenge from step 25 by citing opposing authorities.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Relies on a different set of authorities who disagree
steps.terutzHavaAmina: עולא acted against the accepted ruling of רב and שמואל.
steps.terutzMaskana: עולא followed רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש, who permit a damaged platform.

steps.title: Why a broken platform is different from a broken idol
steps.stepSummary: Even someone who holds that people worship broken idols would agree that a broken platform is permitted, because people just replace it.
steps.simpleTranslation: And even according to the one who says people worship broken pieces, that applies only to the idol itself. Since the person already worshipped it, it is degrading for him to cancel it. But with these platforms, people take the broken one away and bring a different platform.
steps.whatsHappening: עולא now answers רב יהודה's second point from step 26. He explains why the rule about worshipping broken pieces works for an idol but not for a platform.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With an idol, the worshipper already bowed to it, so he feels it would be shameful to throw it away just because it broke. He keeps treating it as a god. A platform was never the object of worship itself, so when it breaks, the worshippers simply replace it, and the broken one loses its status.

keyTerms.meaning: It is a degrading or shameful thing for him
To cancel it, to remove its idol status

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up a clear idea: a broken item stays forbidden only if the worshipper would keep serving it. If he would replace it, the broken item becomes permitted.

phrases.english: And even according to the one who says
they worship broken pieces,
that applies only to the idol itself,
because since he worshipped it,
it is degrading for him to cancel it,
but with these platforms, they take this one away
and bring another platform.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב יהודה's blocking argument from step 26.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Draws a distinction between the idol and its platform
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A broken platform should stay forbidden, just like a broken idol.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only the worshipped idol keeps its status when broken. A platform gets replaced, so the broken one is permitted.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that a damaged platform is permitted, while a damaged altar stays forbidden until most of it is torn down.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is taught in a ברייתא in line with רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש: a platform that was damaged is permitted. An altar that was damaged is forbidden until most of it is torn down.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that supports עולא's sources, רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says the same thing about a platform: once damaged, it is permitted. It also adds something new. An idol altar is stricter: small damage is not enough, and it stays forbidden until most of it is destroyed.

keyTerms.meaning: It is taught in a ברייתא in agreement with him
An altar (here, one used for idol worship)
That most of it is torn down

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up a platform and an altar. They sound alike, but the ברייתא gives them opposite rules when they are damaged.

phrases.english: It is taught in a baraita in line with
Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish:
A platform that was damaged is permitted,
an altar that was damaged is forbidden
until most of it is torn down.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא כְּוָותֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן וְרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the view עולא relied on in steps 27 and 28.
steps.raayaObject: The ruling of רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש that a damaged platform is permitted
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא that permits a damaged platform but forbids a damaged altar until most of it is destroyed

steps.title: What is a platform and what is an altar?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how to tell a platform apart from an altar.
steps.simpleTranslation: What counts as a platform, and what counts as an altar?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a clarifying question. It is setting up the next step, which will define the two terms.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא just gave a platform and an altar different rules. To use those rules, we need to know how the two objects differ.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? What does it look like?

phrases.english: What counts as a platform,
what counts as an altar?

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי דָּמֵי בִּימוֹס, הֵיכִי דָּמֵי מִזְבֵּחַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for definitions of the two terms used in the ברייתא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The physical difference between a בימוס and a מזבח

steps.title: One stone versus many stones
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן explains that a platform is a single stone, while an altar is made of many stones.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יעקב בר אידי said in the name of רבי יוחנן: a platform is one stone, and an altar is many stones.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. A platform is made of one stone, and an altar is built from many stones.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This explains the different rules. A single stone that gets chipped is simply replaced, so it is permitted. An altar built from many stones still stands as an altar after small damage, so it stays forbidden until most of it is torn down.
steps.whatToRemember: A damaged בימוס (one stone) is permitted, because worshippers replace it. A damaged מזבח (many stones) stays forbidden until most of it is destroyed. Even according to the view that broken idols are still worshipped, a broken platform is permitted.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi said
that Rabbi Yochanan said:
A platform is one stone,
an altar is many stones.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יַעֲקֹב בַּר אִידֵּי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the question of step 30.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A בימוס is one stone. A מזבח is built of many stones.
